name: Highland Park Autonomous Zone
description:
Highland Park was already a city within a city — an incorporated enclave like Hamtramck, but without Hamtramck's community cohesion or economic base. When Chrysler left in the 1990s, it took the tax base with it. When the water was shut off in the 2010s, it took the pretense of municipal services. When the Corporate Sovereignty Acts passed in the 2040s, no corponation bothered to claim Highland Park because there was nothing to claim. Three square miles of crumbling infrastructure, contaminated soil, and 8,000 people who couldn't afford to leave. The corponations didn't conquer Highland Park. They simply decided it wasn't worth conquering.

What grew in that vacuum is the HPAZ — the Highland Park Autonomous Zone, an unincorporated, ungoverned, and officially non-existent territory that has become the GLM's most radical experiment in post-corporate living. The HPAZ has no government, no police force, no tax structure, and no formal economy. What it has is a network of mutual aid collectives, squatter communities, urban homesteaders, anarchist tech cooperatives, and approximately 11,000 people who are building something that doesn't have a name yet because naming it would require agreeing on what it is. The old Chrysler headquarters — a brutalist concrete campus that has been slowly colonized by residents, workshops, and a hydroponic farm that fills the former executive parking garage — serves as the closest thing the HPAZ has to a center.

The zone is dangerous. There is no emergency response infrastructure. Medical care is provided by volunteer medics with varying degrees of training. Disputes are resolved through community mediation or, when mediation fails, through means that range from social ostracism to violence. The power grid is a patchwork of stolen connections, solar installations, and a biomass generator that runs on organic waste and smells exactly like you'd expect. But the HPAZ is also genuinely free in a way that nowhere else in the GLM is. No corporate surveillance. No tier classification. No neural interface monitoring. No jurisdiction of any kind. For the people who live here, that freedom is worth everything it costs. For the people who visit, the costs are usually more apparent than the freedom.

sights: The old Chrysler HQ campus — brutalist concrete colonized by murals, gardens, solar panels, and human habitation
Streets where the pavement has been torn up for community gardens, creating a patchwork of asphalt and soil
Makeshift structures built from salvaged materials — architectural improvisation as a way of life
The biomass generator's exhaust stack, wrapped in protest art and trailing a permanent vapor plume
No corporate logos. No advertisements. No holographic signage. The visual silence is disorienting after anywhere else in the GLM.
sounds: Community radio broadcasting on salvaged equipment — news, music, dispute mediation, and emergency alerts
Construction — the HPAZ is always building, always modifying, always making do
Arguments — governance by consensus means everything is debated, loudly, at length
The biomass generator's low chug — unreliable, essential, and loved the way you love something ugly that keeps you alive
Quiet. Real quiet. Not the engineered silence of Geartown but the quiet of a place where the machines that make ambient noise were never installed.
smells: The biomass generator — organic waste processing is not a fragrant operation
Community gardens and hydroponic operations — green, growing things in soil that was declared dead
Woodsmoke from heating systems that use whatever burns
The absence of corporate air processing — the air smells like air, for better and worse
atmosphere.feel: Raw. The HPAZ feels like a wound that's healing into something new — not what was there before, but not scar tissue either. It's uncomfortable, unpredictable, and occasionally dangerous. It's also the only place in the GLM where you can stand on a street corner and not be a data point in someone's optimization model. That feeling — of being genuinely unobserved — is so rare in 2200 that people cry the first time they experience it.

demographics: Approximately 11,000 residents. No demographic data is collected because there is no authority to collect it. Observed population includes anarchist collectives (predominantly white, young, educated), Black families who have lived in Highland Park for generations, climate refugees, corporate dropouts, and people who are hiding from things they don't discuss. The HPAZ does not ask who you were. It only asks what you'll contribute.
economy: Post-monetary in aspiration, barter-and-favor in practice. No formal currency is used. Labor is exchanged directly — I fix your roof, you teach my kid to read. Skilled trades are the highest-value currency: medical training, augment repair, agricultural knowledge, and construction skills. Estimated annual economic activity: incalculable, because the HPAZ doesn't use units the formal economy recognizes.
power_structure: None, formally. In practice, influence concentrates around competence — the people who can fix the generator, treat the sick, and mediate disputes hold informal authority. The Chrysler campus community has the largest population concentration and therefore the most organizational weight. Tensions between the anarchist collectives' ideological frameworks and the legacy residents' practical governance needs are the HPAZ's most persistent internal conflict.
dangers: No emergency services — medical emergencies, fires, and violence are handled by whoever is nearby and willing
Internal conflict — without formal governance, disputes can escalate unpredictably
Contaminated soil — Chrysler's industrial legacy is in the ground, and not all areas have been tested
Predatory elements — the absence of law attracts people who want freedom and people who want victims
External intervention — the HPAZ exists because the corps ignore it, and that could change at any time
opportunities: True anonymity — the HPAZ is the only place in the Detroit metro where surveillance doesn't exist
Experimental technology — the tech cooperatives build things here that couldn't exist under corporate patent law
Disappearance — for people who need to stop existing in corporate databases, the HPAZ is the destination
Community skills — the mutual aid networks teach practical survival skills that corporate education abandoned
story_hooks: A tech cooperative in the Chrysler campus has built a neural interface jammer that creates a 200-meter dead zone around the user — Tessera and Cinderblock AI both want it destroyed, and they're not coordinating, which creates opportunities
Someone is quietly buying the contaminated land around the HPAZ's borders. The purchases are routed through seven shell companies. The endgame is unclear but the encirclement is geometric.

A legacy resident — someone whose family has lived in Highland Park since the 1960s — is dying, and their knowledge of the underground infrastructure (tunnels, sealed basements, utility connections) is dying with them
frequented_by: Anarchist collectives and mutual aid organizers
People who need to disappear from corporate databases
Tech cooperative engineers building outside patent law
Legacy residents who were here before the corps and the anarchists both

notable_locations.name: The Chrysler Campus
notable_locations.description: Former corporate headquarters, now a colonized concrete ecosystem — residences, workshops, a hydroponic farm in the parking garage, and the closest thing the HPAZ has to a town square

notable_locations.name: The Biomass Generator
notable_locations.description: The HPAZ's power source — an ugly, essential machine that converts organic waste into electricity and the surrounding air into an experience

notable_locations.name: The Free Clinic
notable_locations.description: A volunteer medical operation in a converted auto parts store — understaffed, undersupplied, and the only healthcare available for 11,000 people
